intro: A melody has to sing through a storm of repeated piano chords in this E♭ minor study. Karine Gilanyan plays the fifth of Rachmaninoff’s Op. 39 Études-tableaux, whose fierce opening eventually finds a quiet E♭ major ending.

sections.label: A · Melody above repeated chords
sections.mNote: Appassionato; the tune is marked molto marcato

sections.label: B · A song over broken chords
sections.mNote: The left hand opens into flowing sextuplets

sections.label: A′ · The melody moves below
sections.mNote: Tempo I, pesante; repeated chords above a lower melody

sections.label: Coda · Broken chords and a softer song
sections.mNote: The right hand sings dolce towards E♭ major

cues.title: A tune against the chords
cues.text: Appassionato, and then a second instruction: molto marcato, strongly marked. The long upper notes have to carry across repeated triplet chords. Even with two hands full, the pianist has a single line to sing.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 63: Appassionato, molto marcato, sustained melody and chordal triplets. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f5/IMSLP39591-PMLP01894-Rachmaninoff-Etudes-Op39.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last Russian studies
cues.text: Rachmaninoff writes these studies in 1916–17. Before the end of 1917 he leaves Russia for good. The nine pieces of Op. 39 stand at the end of his Russian years, before concert touring becomes his livelihood abroad.
cues.evidence: Nigel Simeone’s Phillips Collection notes date Op. 39 to 1916–17 and place it before Rachmaninoff’s permanent departure after the October Revolution. The composer biography documents his subsequent touring career. https://www.phillipscollection.org/event/2016-11-12-vadym-kholodenko-0

cues.title: The left hand opens
cues.text: The repeated chords loosen into flowing sextuplets in the left hand. Above them, the right hand sings in long notes, marked p. There is suddenly room between the bass and the melody.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 65, third system onwards: piano melody above left-hand sextuplets.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tune in the bass
cues.text: Tempo I, pesante: the opening comes back heavily. This time the melody lies below the repeated chords, in the left hand, again marked molto marcato. The right hand keeps hammering above it.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 68: Tempo I, pesante, lower melody marked molto marcato and repeated upper chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A softer song returns
cues.text: The left hand returns to broken chords and the right hand recovers its singing voice. The score asks for dolce, sweetly. Long notes hang above the accompaniment as the closing pages grow quieter.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed pp. 69–70: quieter broken-chord accompaniment and the dolce melody on p. 70.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E♭ major, dying away
cues.text: E♭ major replaces the minor key of the opening. The last page is marked morendo, dying away: broken chords continue beneath the held upper notes until the hands come to rest.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 71: E♭ major closing harmony, ritardando, morendo and pp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The left hand starts to flow
transitions.to: B · A song over broken chords
transitions.how: A diminuendo takes the force out of the repeated chords. The left hand begins sextuplets in the low bass, opening the chord across the keyboard; the right hand waits, then brings in a quiet melody. Both hands are marked p.
transitions.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 65, second and third systems: diminuendo, low bass and piano sextuplet accompaniment.

transitions.title: The melody drops beneath the chords
transitions.from: B · A song over broken chords
transitions.how: Accelerando and a crescendo drive the chords forward; a ritenuto pulls them back before Tempo I. The opening melody returns in the left hand, marked molto marcato, while the right hand repeats heavy chords. The bass reaches down to E♭.
transitions.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 68: accelerando, crescendo, ritenuto, Tempo I and pesante.

transitions.title: The singing hand rises again
transitions.to: Coda · Broken chords and a softer song
transitions.how: The right hand leaves its repeated chords and takes up the melody again. The left hand spreads the harmony into broken chords; p and then dolce replace the heavy return’s instructions. These flowing figures carry the closing pages towards E♭ major and the final morendo.
transitions.evidence: Piano score, printed pp. 69–71: piano broken chords, dolce melody and E♭ major morendo ending.

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
